questions.prompt: Write the gain-bandwidth product, in radians per second, of a common-source stage whose load capacitance CL sets the dominant pole. The midband gain magnitude is gm times the resistance at the drain. Use gm and CL.
questions.explanation: The gain magnitude is \(g_m R\) and the output pole is \(1/(RC_L)\), so the product is \(g_m/C_L\). The resistance cancels. Keeping \(R\) in the product, as \(g_m R/C_L\), still has the load in it and is not the gain-bandwidth. \(1/(RC_L)\) is the pole alone. The input Miller time constant uses the source resistance and the device capacitances; it is not this product. Halving the drain resistance doubles the bandwidth and halves the gain, and the product stays put.

questions.prompt: A worked solution halves the drain resistance of a common-source stage whose bandwidth is set by a large load capacitance. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: Bandwidth and gain trade one for one when the load capacitance dominates. Their product is \(g_m/C_L\), which has no drain resistance in it. Raising the product means raising \(g_m\) or lowering the load capacitance. The input pole does not set this trade while the load capacitance is the large one.
steps: The dominant pole sits at the output, at \(1/[(R_D\parallel r_o)C_L]\).
Halving \(R_D\parallel r_o\) doubles that pole frequency.
The midband gain magnitude is \(g_m(R_D\parallel r_o)\), so the same cut halves the gain.
Gain and bandwidth therefore both double, and the gain-bandwidth product rises by four.
reasons: The gain falls by the same factor the bandwidth rises, so \(g_m/C_L\) is unchanged.
Halving the load resistance moves the pole down, because a smaller resistance drives the capacitor more slowly.

questions.prompt: Order why a source follower is the cheaper way to drive a large load capacitance at the same gain and a higher bandwidth. Each step after the first uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The follower moves the load capacitance off the high-resistance node without giving up the gain. Cutting the drain resistance and raising the common-source \(g_m\) to hold the product spends that current in the gain device. The follower does not multiply the load by a Miller factor. Ignoring the follower's own output pole leaves out the new time constant \(C_L/g_{m2}\).
steps: The common-source stage keeps its drain resistance, so it keeps the gain \(g_m(R_D\parallel r_o)\).
Its drain now sees the follower's small input capacitance instead of the load capacitance.
The load capacitance is driven by the follower's output resistance, about \(1/g_{m2}\), far below the drain resistance.
The extra current is one follower branch. Holding the gain while cutting the drain resistance instead would raise the common-source current in proportion.
